evidence: Plin. Ep. 1.15.1: prōmittis ad cēnam, nec venīs?
terms.comment: With an accusative, or a future infinitive: prōmittō mē ventūrum esse, I promise I’ll come. Prōmittere ad cēnam, to promise to come to dinner (Lewis & Short). The noun, a promise, is prōmissum; one’s word, fidēs (see word, promise).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.5.1: quam eram solitus dē meā pollicērī
Traupman 106: nihil certī polliceor, I’m not making any definite promise
Sall. J. 23.2: multa pollicendō (Lewis & Short s.v. cōnfirmō)
Traupman 106: to make many promises, multa pollicērī
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to hold forth, offer, promise”; often of what one offers to do for someone.

evidence: Plaut. Capt. 898c–898d: Spondēn' tū istud? — Spondeō.
Cic. Phil. 5.51 (Lewis & Short): prōmittō, recipiō, spondeō
terms.comment: The word of the Roman contract made by question and answer, spondēsne? spondeō (Lewis & Short); also of promising a daughter in marriage.

phrases.latin: heus tū! prōmittis ad cēnam, nec venīs?
phrases.english: Hey, you! You promise to come to dinner, and then you don’t turn up?

phrases.latin: plūs ego polliceor: nīl recitābō tibi
phrases.english: I promise you more: I won’t read you a thing
Do you promise that? — I promise.
